body:
The economic situation at independence

When India became independent in 1947, it inherited a predominantly agricultural economy with widespread poverty, low agricultural productivity, food shortages, inadequate infrastructure and a weak industrial base. Industrial development was concentrated in a limited number of regions. Large sections of the population depended on agriculture, while modern industries, electricity generation, transport and irrigation facilities were insufficient.

Developing such an economy required substantial investment in projects such as dams, power stations, railways, steel plants and heavy machinery. These projects required large amounts of capital and often took many years to become productive. The government therefore assumed a leading role in directing economic development.

Planned development and the mixed economy

Planned development

Planned development means setting national economic priorities, assessing available resources and preparing plans to achieve specific development objectives over a defined period. The government uses public investment, economic policies and regulation to guide the economy.

India adopted a mixed economy, in which the public and private sectors operate together. The government took responsibility for important infrastructure, strategic industries and major capital-intensive projects. Private individuals and companies continued to operate in agriculture, trade, manufacturing and services, subject to government policies and regulations.

India therefore did not adopt a completely state-controlled economy. Nor did it leave economic development entirely to private enterprise. It combined public investment and private economic activity.

Four major objectives of economic planning

  • Growth: Increase national income, production and the productive capacity of the economy.
  • Modernisation: Introduce improved technology, modern production methods and better economic institutions.
  • Self-reliance: Develop domestic productive capacity and reduce excessive dependence on imported food, machinery and industrial goods. Self-reliance did not mean complete isolation from international trade.
  • Equity: Reduce poverty, economic inequality and concentration of wealth while improving opportunities for disadvantaged groups and backward regions.

These objectives were connected but could sometimes conflict. For example, mechanisation could increase agricultural production while reducing the demand for certain types of manual labour. Similarly, investment in heavy industries could support long-term growth but compete with immediate requirements for agricultural development. Planning involved balancing such priorities.

Institutions responsible for national planning

Planning Commission

The Government of India established the Planning Commission on 15 March 1950 through an executive resolution. It was an extra-constitutional and non-statutory body; neither the Constitution nor a parliamentary Act created it.

The Prime Minister served as its Chairperson. Its principal responsibilities included assessing the country's material, financial and human resources, identifying development priorities, preparing Five-Year Plans and evaluating their implementation.

National Development Council

The National Development Council (NDC) was established in 1952 to strengthen cooperation between the Union and State governments in economic planning. It was chaired by the Prime Minister and included State Chief Ministers and other important government representatives. It provided a forum for discussing national development priorities and coordinating State participation in the plans.

Replacement by NITI Aayog

On 1 January 2015, the Government of India established the NITI Aayog, replacing the Planning Commission. NITI Aayog functions as a policy think tank and promotes cooperative federalism by encouraging participation of States in national development strategies. Its approach emphasises policy coordination, strategic planning and long-term development rather than the earlier Planning Commission model of centralised Five-Year Plan formulation.

Important distinction

Planned development describes the government's role in setting economic priorities. A mixed economy describes the coexistence of public and private ownership. India adopted both approaches together.

Prelims focus

  • The Planning Commission was established on 15 March 1950 by executive resolution.
  • The Planning Commission was neither a constitutional nor a statutory body.
  • The National Development Council was established in 1952.
  • India adopted a mixed economy with both public and private sectors.
  • NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
  • Trap: Planned development did not mean complete government ownership of all industries.

[Sources: NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class XII Political Science, Chapter 12, Politics of Planned Development, pp. 49–63; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class XI Economics, Chapter 2, Indian Economy 1950–1990, pp. 17–31; Government of India, Resolution establishing the Planning Commission, 15 March 1950; NITI Aayog, Cabinet Resolution establishing NITI Aayog, 1 January 2015; Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Statistical Year Book India, Five-Year Plans. Online government sources consulted on 22 November 2026.]

body:
The first three Five-Year Plans

Five-Year Plans became the principal instruments through which the Government of India organised public investment and pursued economic development. Each plan had a defined period and emphasised particular sectors according to the country's economic requirements.

PlanPeriodMain emphasisModel or major event
First Plan1951–1956Agriculture, irrigation, power and community development.Associated with the Harrod–Domar model.
Second Plan1956–1961Heavy industries, capital goods and public-sector expansion.Mahalanobis model.
Third Plan1961–1966Self-reliance, agricultural development and industrial expansion.Disrupted by wars and droughts.
Annual Plans1966–1969Economic stabilisation and agricultural recovery.Known as the Plan Holiday.

First Five-Year Plan: agriculture and irrigation

The First Plan concentrated on agriculture because India faced food shortages and needed to increase agricultural production. Investment was directed towards irrigation, power generation, agricultural improvement, rehabilitation and rural development. Its broad economic approach is commonly associated with the Harrod–Domar growth model, which emphasised the relationship between savings, investment and economic growth.

Second Five-Year Plan: heavy industrialisation

The Second Plan shifted the main emphasis towards heavy and basic industries. It followed the Mahalanobis model, associated with economist P.C. Mahalanobis. The strategy emphasised investment in capital goods industries, such as steel and heavy machinery, because these industries supplied the equipment needed for further industrial development.

Agriculture remained important, but the allocation of resources increasingly favoured industrial expansion. The development of a domestic heavy industrial base was considered essential for long-term self-reliance.

Third Plan and Plan Holiday

The Third Plan aimed to achieve economic self-reliance and strengthen both agriculture and industry. However, the 1962 war with China, the 1965 war with Pakistan and successive drought conditions created serious economic difficulties. Agricultural production declined, food shortages increased and financial resources came under pressure.

Between 1966 and 1969, India implemented three Annual Plans instead of beginning another Five-Year Plan. This period is called the Plan Holiday. It was not a complete suspension of planning. Annual plans continued, and the new agricultural strategy associated with the Green Revolution began during this period.

Community Development Programme

Community development

Community development is an approach to rural development that seeks to improve village life through local participation, self-help, government assistance and coordinated development activities.

The Government of India launched the Community Development Programme on 2 October 1952. Its purpose was to improve the overall economic and social conditions of rural communities rather than concentrating only on agricultural production.

The initial programme covered 55 community development project areas, approximately 25,000 villages and about 16.4 million people. Its activities included:

  • Agricultural improvement, improved seeds and better farming practices.
  • Irrigation, minor water resources and soil improvement.
  • Rural roads, communication and village infrastructure.
  • Primary education, adult education and public health.
  • Sanitation, drinking water and housing improvement.
  • Animal husbandry and cooperative activities.

The programme encouraged villagers to contribute labour and local resources while government agencies supplied technical and administrative assistance.

National Extension Service

The National Extension Service was introduced on 2 October 1953. It extended rural development and agricultural extension activities to a wider geographical area. Compared with the Community Development Programme, it generally provided a less intensive package of assistance to each covered area.

Balwantrai Mehta Committee and Panchayati Raj

The Community Development Programme faced difficulties because government administration often dominated local decision-making and people's participation was insufficient. The Government appointed the Balwantrai Mehta Committee in 1957 to examine the working of community development and national extension programmes.

The committee recommended democratic decentralisation through a three-tier Panchayati Raj system:

  • Village level: Gram Panchayat, responsible for local village administration and development.
  • Block level: Panchayat Samiti, coordinating development programmes across villages and serving as the executive body.
  • District level: Zila Parishad, coordinating development activities at the district level.

Rajasthan became the first State to introduce the Panchayati Raj system at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. The 73rd Constitutional Amendment, 1992, later gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions through Part IX of the Constitution, effective from 24 April 1993.

Do not confuse these institutions

The Community Development Programme was a rural development programme. The National Extension Service expanded extension activities. Panchayati Raj created elected local self-government institutions to strengthen people's participation in development.

Multipurpose river valley projects

Large dams and river valley projects became important instruments of planned development. A multipurpose river valley project uses river water and associated infrastructure to achieve several objectives rather than serving only one purpose.

A typical project may include a dam, reservoir, canals, power stations and associated irrigation works. Its objectives may include:

  • Irrigation for agricultural land.
  • Hydroelectric power generation.
  • Flood moderation and water regulation.
  • Drinking and industrial water supply.
  • Navigation, fisheries and other economic activities.

Important projects and their rivers

ProjectRiverLocation and chronologyMain purposes
Damodar Valley CorporationDamodarEstablished 7 July 1948; Jharkhand and West Bengal.Flood control, irrigation, power and regional development.
Bhakra–NangalSutlejProject taken up in 1948; main dam dedicated in 1963; Himachal Pradesh and Punjab.Irrigation and hydroelectric power.
HirakudMahanadiOdisha; inaugurated in 1957.Flood control, irrigation and power generation.
Sardar SarovarNarmadaFoundation stone laid on 5 April 1961; Gujarat and three other participating States.Irrigation, drinking water and hydroelectric power.

The Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) was established in 1948 and became India's first major integrated multipurpose river valley development corporation. The Bhakra-Nangal project was taken up in 1948. Its irrigation channels began supplying water in 1954, before the main dam was dedicated by Jawaharlal Nehru on 22 October 1963.

The Hirakud Dam was constructed across the Mahanadi in Odisha and inaugurated in 1957. The Sardar Sarovar Project is an important Gujarat connection. It is an interstate multipurpose project involving Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. Its foundation stone was laid on 5 April 1961, and it was intended to provide irrigation, drinking water and electricity.

Jawaharlal Nehru described Bhakra as the new temple of resurgent India, reflecting the importance attached to large dams in the early development strategy.

Benefits and limitations of large dams

Large dams expanded irrigation and electricity generation and helped regulate river flows. However, they also created serious social and environmental problems. Reservoirs submerged agricultural land, forests and settlements, requiring the displacement and rehabilitation of affected communities. Changes in river flow affected downstream ecosystems, while excessive irrigation in some command areas contributed to waterlogging and soil salinity. Benefits and costs were not always distributed equally among regions and communities.

Project chronology matters

The Damodar Valley Corporation dates to 1948, Hirakud was inaugurated in 1957, the Sardar Sarovar foundation stone was laid in 1961, and the Bhakra main dam was dedicated in 1963. These dates refer to different stages of the projects.

Prelims focus

  • First Plan: 1951–1956, agriculture and irrigation; Second Plan: 1956–1961, heavy industry.
  • First Plan: Harrod–Domar association; Second Plan: Mahalanobis model.
  • Community Development Programme: 2 October 1952; National Extension Service: 2 October 1953.
  • Balwantrai Mehta Committee: 1957; first Panchayati Raj launch: Nagaur, Rajasthan, 2 October 1959.
  • DVC: Damodar, 1948; Hirakud: Mahanadi, 1957; Bhakra-Nangal: Sutlej; Sardar Sarovar: Narmada.
  • Trap: The Plan Holiday of 1966–1969 contained Annual Plans; it was not a period without planning.

[Sources: NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class XII Political Science, Chapter 12, pp. 49–63; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class XII Geography, Chapter 6, Water Resources, pp. 60–71; Government of India, Community Development Programme in India, NITI Aayog Digital Library; Yojana, National Extension Service, 1957; Ministry of Panchayati Raj, historical account of the Balwantrai Mehta Committee and Panchayati Raj; Damodar Valley Corporation, official history; Bhakra Beas Management Board, Bhakra Project History; Odisha Review, Hirakud Dam history; Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Limited, project history. Online sources consulted on 22 November 2026.]
